OPEN
This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Let $f(n)$ be minimal such that, for any $A=\{a_1,\ldots,a_n\}\subseteq [2,\infty)\cap\mathbb{N}$ of size $n$, in any interval $I$ of $f(n)\max(A)$ consecutive integers there exist distinct $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in I$ such that $a_i\mid x_i$.
Obtain good bounds for $f(n)$, or even an asymptotic formula.
#709: [ErSu59][Er92c]
number theory
A problem of Erdős and Surányi [ErSu59], who proved\[(\log n)^c \ll f(n) \ll n^{1/2}\]for some constant $c>0$. The lower bound here can be improved, using van Doorn's lower bound for [711] from [vD26], to\[\frac{\log n}{\log\log n}\ll f(n).\]See also [708].
Additional thanks to: Zeraoulia Rafik and Terence Tao

 I do not know how to solve the problem completely, but there is a simple improvement $
f(n)\gg {\log n\over \log\log n}
$.
Let $F(n,m)$ denote the least integer $L$ such that the interval $(m,m+L]$ contains distinct multiples of $1,2,\dots,n$.
For the set $A=\{2,\dots,n\}$, the defining property of $f(n)$ implies $F(n,m)\le f(n)n$ for every $m$. On the other hand, van Doorn proved that for all sufficiently large $n$ there exists $m=m(n)$ such that $
F(n,m)\gg n{\log n\over \log\log n}.$ Combining the two inequalities gives the claim.
It is natural to guess that the truth is much closer to the lower bound than to the upper bound.
Disclosure statement :Based on @Prof Tao comment,I have used Chatgpt thinking 5.4 for help and for the above combination
[ErPo80] P. Erdős and C. Pomerance, Matching the natural numbers up to $n$ with distinct multiples in another interval, Indag. Math. 42 (1980), 147–151.
[vD26] W. van Doorn, On the length of an interval that contains distinct multiples of the first $n$ positive integers, arXiv:2601.16972, 2026.

 The main points of the above remark can be summarized as follows:
the lower bound of Erdős-Surányi proof (which gives $c = 1 - \frac{1 + \log \log 2}{\log 2} \approx 0.086$) can be improved to $f(n) \gg \frac{\log n}{\log \log n}$ by restricting to the special case $A = \{2, 3, \ldots, n+1\}$ and using van Doorn's bound on #711. If one instead uses the results of [ErPo80], one already obtains the intermediate lower bound $f(n) \gg \sqrt{\log n/\log\log n}$. (These observations were obtained from conversation with Wouter and GPT.)
As a reminder, all use of AI tools need to be disclosed, and unnecessarily lengthy AI-generated text should be avoided in the comments to this forum; replacement with a shorter human-generated summary is strongly preferred.
